clusters.title: Mississippi Senate race is toss-up, with razor-thin margin
clusters.neutral_headline: Mississippi Senate race is toss-up, with razor-thin margin

items.title: Mississippi Senate race is toss-up, with razor-thin margin
items.standfirst: The Senate race in deep-red Mississippi remains unresolved Thursday morning, as Democrat Scott Colom has mounted a surprisingly competitive challenge to incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.
items.content: The Senate race in deep-red Mississippi remains unresolved Thursday morning, as Democrat Scott Colom has mounted a surprisingly competitive challenge to incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.

items.title: How the Mississippi Senate Race Became a Nail-Biter
items.standfirst: Eyes are on the closely divided race, where Democratic challenger Scott Colom is leading GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by a razor-thin margin.
items.content: District Attorney and U.S. Senate candidate for Mississippi Scott Colom speaks as he gives an update on state of Senate race against Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Jackson, Mississippi, on Nov. 4, 2026. —Rogelio V. Solis—Getty ImagesAs Democrats are celebrating a historic blue wave, eyes are on the Senate race in deep-red Mississippi, where the Democratic candidate led the Republican incumbent by a razor-thin margin of 1,138 votes as of Wednesday evening.The Associated Press has not yet called the race because it is so close, with Democratic challenger Scott Colom ahead by about 0.1%—he has so far earned 49% of the vote compared to Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith’s 48.9%, with 96% of votes counted. It’s a stunning nail-biter of a race that, in the weeks leading up to Election Day, polls had suggested would likely be won by the Republican incumbent by a narrow margin.“I can’t recall the last time it’s been this close for a statewide Senate contest—or a statewide election in general,” says Aaron Hitefield, an assistant professor of political science at Mississippi State University. “It’s unprecedented for [Mississippi] to be this competitive for Democrats particularly, certainly in the last 40 years.”Read More: What Democrats’ Midterm Gains Reveal About Trump’s Voter CoalitionPolitical experts say it could take a few days before the outcome of the race becomes clear.If Colom, a district attorney, wins the race, it would be the first time that Mississippi voters have elected a Democrat to represent them in the U.S. Senate since 1982. A Democratic victory would also be a remarkable shift in a state that President Donald Trump won by a nearly 23-point margin just two years ago. Such an upset would cap off a string of staggering victories for Democrats, who have so far flipped seven seats in the upper chamber in this year’s midterm elections, including in other staunchly red states like Texas and South Carolina.Both candidates appeared to be optimistic that the election would ultimately go their way, though they also acknowledged that the race is still too close to call. Colom said in a statement early Wednesday morning, “I am confident we will ultimately flip this seat.”“The results are all trending in our direction,” Colom said in a speech to his supporters on Election Night. “The reality is, though, we’re not going to get the results tonight. I’m excited about our momentum, I’m excited about where we are.”Speaking to a crowd of her supporters on Election Night, Hyde-Smith said she was confident that she would hold her seat in the upper chamber.“We still don’t have all the votes in, so we’re not calling all of it tonight, but we’re in a very good lead and I assure you, I will continue to be your U.S. Senator,” she said.When asked about Hyde-Smith’s speech at a press conference on Wednesday, Colom replied, “Bless her heart.”When will we know who won the Mississippi Senate race?It is possible that the winner of the Senate contest may not be determined until the end of the week—or even next week. The state has five business days after Election Day to count affidavit ballots. An individual would turn in such a ballot, which is also called a provisional ballot, in a situation in which they believe they’re eligible and registered to vote but are unable to cast a standard ballot—for instance, if their name is not in their local polling place’s records. These votes are only counted once election workers verify the individual’s information. Mississippi also permits mail-in ballots that arrive within five days after Election Day, so long as they were postmarked by Election Day, to be counted.All this means that it’s possible the race may not be called until a week after Election Day, says Emily Ommundsen, an assistant professor of political science at the University of Mississippi.“Because of the razor-thin margins we currently see, I don’t expect any results to be called before then,” Ommundsen says.How did the Mississippi Senate race become such a tight contest?The tight race in Mississippi is one of many that illustrate the extremely challenging political environment Republicans have faced this year. Historically, the party in the White House loses seats in midterm elections, and that pressure on Republicans was compounded in this election cycle because of historically low approval for Trump driven in large part by the economy, as well as the war in Iran.Ommundsen says that, while ballots are still being counted, the result in Mississippi, so far, “is consistent with trends that we saw nationally.”“Nearly all counties that had a Senate election on the ballot moved towards the left compared to how they voted in 2024,” she says, though she notes that there are some exceptions. “Mississippi just happens to be one of those elections that was closer and perhaps more ripe for a flip.”Hitefield likens this year’s midterms to “a referendum on the President,” adding that “Democrats were turning out to oppose the President and to oppose the President’s policies.”But he cautions that the close contest in Mississippi is not necessarily a sign that the deep-red state is turning blue or even purple. It’s possible, he says, that Republican voters didn’t cast their ballots for a Democrat, and instead stayed home.“I wouldn’t necessarily read in, long story short, to Mississippi becoming a Georgia—you know, being a fully competitive every election state,” Hitefield says. “But I think it’s certainly moving toward a state that you shouldn’t sleep on when it comes to electoral competitiveness.”Hitefield also says that there’s a lot of “voter apathy” within the Republican party with regards to Hyde-Smith, and she hasn’t performed as well as Mississippi’s other Republican Senator, Roger Wicker, in past elections. Wicker won his re-election bid in 2024 by a more than 25-point margin. Hyde-Smith, meanwhile, won her re-election fight in 2020 by about 10 points.Hitefield adds that Hyde-Smith had some “gaffes” during the campaign, when she made some remarks about the rising cost of living that some voters felt were dismissive. For instance, when asked about soaring costs, including beef prices, during an interview with WLOX in February, Hyde-Smith applauded the passing of Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill and went on to say, “It is on everybody’s mind. It is certainly me at my house. And you know, you have so many proteins to choose from. And all commodities go through peaks and valleys.”National polling ahead of Election Day indicated that an overwhelming majority of American voters felt that the economy was a crucial issue for them heading into this year’s midterms.Colom’s campaign jumped on Hyde-Smith’s remark, releasing an ad in which people objected to Hyde-Smith’s comment, including one who said in the video, “Pick another protein? Sh**, I’d rather pick another Senator instead.” The ad racked up more than 7.5 million views on Colom’s X account.Ommundsen points out that Hyde-Smith didn’t make many public campaign appearances in this year’s election cycle; one of the few appearances the Senator made was last week, when she gave very brief remarks at a rally the President held for her in Mississippi.Hitefield says Hyde-Smith didn’t “do the groundwork necessary to run a successful campaign” in this election cycle.“I think that it was a real mistake by her campaign, regardless of what the outcome looks like at the end of this,” Hitefield says. “Even if she does win, she didn’t do, really, what she needed to win with any sort of safety. I think that’s something [where] if she does win, she’ll need to think about, moving forward, how to strategize more effectively.”Colom, on the other hand, ran a “successful campaign” and generated “so much voter excitement,” Hitefield says—so much so that it stirred “this groundswell of hopes within the Democratic party that this seat could be flipped.”If Colom wins, he would also become the first Black Senator from Mississippi since the 19th century—the last time the state sent a Black lawmaker to the upper chamber was during Reconstruction in the aftermath of the Civil War.“It would be an unprecedented outcome when it comes to the history of Mississippi,” Hitefield says.

items.title: CBS News exit polls show how Democrats won in the midterms
items.standfirst: Economic issues helped propel President Trump to victory in 2024, and those same issues dragged down his party in 2026.
items.content: Economic issues helped propel President Trump to victory in 2024, and those same issues dragged down his party in 2026.

items.title: What Democrats’ Midterm Gains Reveal About Trump’s Voter Coalition
items.standfirst: Democrats gained ground with groups that helped power President Donald Trump’s 2024 win, amid frustration with the economy and his presidency.
items.content: Ariana Cuevas, a 19-year-old student, shows off her sticker after voting for the first time, while her boyfriend photographs the moment. —Mindy Schauer—MediaNewsGroup/Orange County Register via Getty ImagesThe 2026 midterm elections saw historic gains for Democrats, who won control of both chambers of Congress and flipped key seats in states like Texas, Kansas, and South Carolina. The electorate’s leftward swing was diverse and widespread, but three demographics showed notable shifts that helped support Democrats on Tuesday.Distinct gains came from young, rural, and Hispanic voters—all of whom were key to President Donald Trump’s victory in 2024. National polling on how these groups voted in House races offers a broad measure of their support for Democrats, while Senate contests reveal how those trends played out in key states. Experts weigh in on what may have prompted the shifts.Read more: Inside the Democrats' Plans to Take On TrumpYoung votersYoung people overwhelmingly supported Democratic candidates this election cycle. According to the AP Voter Poll, which was conducted Oct. 19 through Nov. 3, about 7 in 10 voters ages 18 to 29 said they supported the Democratic candidate in their local House races, while about 3 in 10 said they voted Republican. Although Trump was not on the ballot, the poll found that 60% of young voters said their House vote was intended to “express opposition to Donald Trump.” This marks a sharp change from the presidential election in 2024, when Trump won an estimated 39% of young voters, making historic gains among the demographic. But the Republican Party was unable to capitalize on those gains just two years later.Outside of commentary on the President, 43% of young voters said that their top issue was the economy. Santiago Mayer, the executive director of Voters of Tomorrow, tells TIME that young people felt “betrayed” by Trump’s economic policies.“Young people trusted Donald Trump to bring prices down and work on affordability,” the 24-year-old explains. “He betrayed everything that he told us: He made prices higher with tariffs, he did not work on housing, and he started an illegal war.”Mayer says that while it's undeniable that Trump won over young men in 2024, he did so at the time with a $1.2 billion investment in youth in the five years preceding 2024, outspending the left 10 to 1.“The difference this year is that the money just didn’t cut it, there was a misread by Republicans of what drove young people toward them in 2024,” he says, claiming that Trump had targeted young men at a time when they felt particularly “left behind.” This year, it was the opposition that was able to best speak to those sentiments. If Democrats are to retain the support they won in this election, however, Mayer says they will need to deliver in Congress.“Democrats got the trust of young people this time, so they need to deliver, or else they might swing again, or stay on the couch for the next election,” he says, pointing out that the latest data, which is still being tallied, already shows that Gen Z is on track to either match or exceed its record turnout in 2018, the first year for which the generation was eligible to vote. “Young people need to be able to afford the lives they were promised by older generations,” he says. Hispanic votersAbout 6 in 10 Hispanic voters said they chose the Democratic candidate in their local House race in 2026, according to the AP Voter Poll. In Texas, they were particularly instrumental in flipping the open Senate seat. Roughly 6 in 10 Hispanic voters in the Texas Senate race supported Democrat James Talarico, compared to just 3 in 10 who supported Trump-endorsed Republican Ken Paxton.Stephanie Valencia, a co-founder of Equis Research, tells TIME that one of the big takeaways from Tuesday’s midterms was how consequential the Hispanic vote has become in America.“Key takeaway from last night is that Latinos are the key swing voter,” she says. “People love to call the Latino vote the ‘sleeping giant,’ but we are the swinging giant.”The latest swing was largely informed by two areas of discontent, according to recent polls: Trump’s presidency overall and, specifically, his handling of the economy.Trump’s approval rating among Latino voters dropped from 38% in February 2025 to 24% in September and October, according to a Pew Research Center poll from last month. Of those who backed him in 2024, the decline was even greater, with approval down from 93% in 2025 to 57% in October. A survey by BSP Research and the African American Research Collaborative found that specific economic grievances included the cost of living and inflation. More than 7 in 10 Latino voters disapproved of Trump’s handling of the economy, according to an AP-NORC poll from October.Valencia says that Tuesday’s vote was a “middle finger to Trump and Republicans and their misplaced promises” from the Hispanic community. It’s the same way they showed dissatisfaction toward Democrats when they supported Trump in 2024, she says, and therefore it should be noted that “while the shifts and the gains are real, they are not necessarily permanent.”“The lesson for Democrats is not to interpret their opponents' loss as their victory,” she says. “The worst they could do is see 2024 as a blip and not see how they are in a probationary period with Latinos.”In 2024, when Trump drew near even with his opponent Kamala Harris among Hispanic voters, Valencia said that the demographic was driven by the same priorities they have expressed in 2026: cost of living, inflation, and immigration.“For both Biden and Trump, the common thread is rising costs and not rising wages,” Valencia says. The challenge for a Democratic-controlled Congress, now, is to figure out how to work with Trump and provide “clear delivery” to Latino voters, she adds.Rural votersTraditionally, there is a large party divide between urban voters and rural voters—with the former overwhelmingly voting for Democrats and the latter more often voting for Republicans.The Pew Research Center shows a pronounced gap in 2024, with nearly 70% of validated voters who described their communities as rural voting for Trump, and 29% voting for Harris.Rural voters still favored Republican candidates in 2026, according to the AP Voter Poll, but the demographic shifted significantly to the left: 57% of rural voters opted for the Republican candidate in the House, versus 41% opting for the Democratic candidate.The shift influenced several key battleground states. In Kansas, for example, Democrat Adam Hamilton was elected to the Senate—the first Democrat sent to the upper chamber from the state in almost 100 years. According to a New York Times analysis of Senate votes in Kansas, every single county—even the rural counties in the northwest of the state, which Trump won in a landslide in 2024—shifted toward Democrats.Hamilton also notably flipped three rural counties in the southwest of the state: Finney, Ford, and Seward counties. According to Alexandra Middlewood, an associate professor of political science at Wichita State University, this flip can at least in part be attributed to unannounced immigration enforcement operations at meatpacking plants in all three of these counties in September. It may have soured locals on the leadership of the Republican Party, she observes.“If we look at those counties, their voter registration increased in the month of September, and that was when those ICE raids were happening,” Middlewood tells TIME. “The correlation is there.”Democrats also flipped 20 seats in the Kansas House of Representatives, which Middlewood calls “insane.”She notes that economic issues are also hitting rural voters in Kansas and across the U.S. in unique ways that might be driving dissatisfaction with the Trump Administration.An AP/KFF poll released in September found that about half of rural American voters believe the economy is worse off than when Trump first returned to office.“I think part of that is just they're paying more for gas because they have to drive cars to travel everywhere,” Middlewood says, pointing to the trend of rising gas prices since the war in Iran began in February. “A lot of those rural areas have farmers and cattle ranchers, and they are paying more for harvest season. So, in general, rural Kansans have been particularly impacted by these economic policies coming out of the Trump Administration.”

clusters.title: Meet the Democratic Rising Stars Who Could Shape 2028
clusters.neutral_headline: Meet the Democratic Rising Stars Who Could Shape 2028

items.title: Meet the Democratic Rising Stars Who Could Shape 2028
items.standfirst: The Democrats' sweeping victory will reshape the final two years of President Donald Trump’s presidency and could have a significant impact on the 2028 presidential map.
items.content: Sen.-elect James Talarico and Texas gov.-elect State Rep. Gina Hinojosa toast with a fountain beverage at a Whataburger restaurant in Austin, Texas, on Nov. 3, 2026. —Brandon Bell—Getty ImagesIn what is widely being referred to as a “blue tsunami,” the Democratic Party won control of both the House and Senate in the midterm elections, gaining ground in deep-red and battleground states. The sweeping victory will reshape the final two years of President Donald Trump’s presidency and could have a significant impact on the 2028 presidential map.In formerly reliably Republican Texas, James Talarico defeated the Trump-backed Ken Paxton and became the first Democrat to be elected Senator by Texans since 1988. Texas state representative Gina Hinojosa pulled off a similar victory, defeating three-term governor Greg Abbott. She will be the state’s first ever Latina governor. Kansas, which Trump won by a margin of 16 points in 2024, elected Adam Hamilton, welcoming its first Democratic senator since 1932.Seth Masket, a professor of political science at the University of Denver, describes the election as “a pretty stunning rebuke of Trump and the Republicans,” one that has given Democrats “a lot more confidence” heading into 2028.With momentum now behind the party, Democrats are already setting their sights on a return to the White House. “Over the next two years, Democrats will show up where Republicans have failed and work every single day to bring down costs. Up next: the White House,” vowed Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin.Yet despite their strong showing at the polls, Democrats still lack a clear leader heading into 2028, setting the stage for what could be a hard-fought primary. There are Democratic heavyweights who often appear on presidential contender lists, including California Gov. Gavin Newsom, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, and former presidential candidate Kamala Harris. However, the Democrats’ midterm victories are a reminder that the party’s rising stars should not be ignored, as they will undoubtedly play an important role in shaping what the 2028 race will look like. Here’s who you need to be aware of as the Democrats prepare to reset Washington: —Chip Somodevilla—Getty ImagesJames TalaricoTalarico’s midterm victory was made even more significant by the margin. He won the state by 12 points, just two years after Trump carried Texas by 14 points, marking a stunning 26-point swing in the Democratic candidate's favor.His victory may well shape how many Democrats run their campaigns in the future.Talarico, 37, a Presbyterian minister-in-training, frequently drew on his Christianity and liberal principles in his speeches, while also touting his record of working alongside Republicans as a Texas state representative. Throughout his campaign, he sought to frame the political divide as top versus bottom, rather than along traditional party lines.“We just showed that a politics of division is no match for a politics of love,” Talarico said in his victory speech in Austin, standing behind a podium that read “Love Thy Neighbour”—a reference to the biblical commandment.“A lot of Democrats will be turning to his example, to the way he ran, the particular style he used,” Masket says, pointing to Talarico's use of liberal Christianity and his emphasis on bipartisanship. “He's definitely on the bench for Democrats in future cycles.”Todd Belt, a professor of political management at the George Washington University, agrees that Talarico’s “common sense themes” and the “plain spoken” way he communicates with voters could be a strong asset ahead of the 2028 race.“Texas has been the big white whale for Democrats, and it's got 40 electoral votes, so it's going to be a big player,” he tells TIME. “Democrats can put Republicans on the defensive there, and somebody like Talarico will be really interesting to watch.” —Erik S. Lesser—Getty ImagesJon OssoffJon Ossoff, delivered one of the strongest Democratic victories in a battleground state, winning re-election and holding the Georgia Senate seat for Democrats, seeing off his Republican challenger Mike Collins. Masket notes how Ossoff, 39, ran a “very national campaign over this past year” by taking his re-election pitch to younger voters through various podcast appearances. He discussed health care and the importance of young people being engaged in politics with Georgia rapper Killer Mike in September and appeared on comedy podcast The 85 South Show in October, where he addressed the key issues facing Atlanta. His strong criticisms of Trump and his Administration have often gone viral on social media. He also made sure to include appearances on mainstream media in the months leading up to his campaign. In a February appearance on Stephen Colbert’s now-defunct late-night show, Ossoff discussed "The Epstein Class," a phrase he uses to refer to the ultra-wealthy and political elites who, he says, are operating as if the rules don't apply to them. “He is seen as having turned Georgia, which was considered a very red state until pretty recently, to become competitive, and now he had a very strong Democratic result here with his election,” says Masket, who believes the victory strengthens Ossoff's standing as a potential presidential contender in 2028.A national polling average from Race to the White House places Ossoff fifth among potential Democratic nominees, at 10.8%. Meanwhile, betting site Polymarket places him first in its market for the party's nomination, giving him a 24% chance of winning.Ossoff, however, had earlier this year ruled out the possibility of a run for the White House, stating: “I am not running for President in 2028. I have no interest in running for President in 2028.” Even if he doesn’t hold presidential ambitions of his own, his impact on the party and its direction will surely be felt as it chooses its contender for the White House. —Sarah Rice—Getty ImagesAbdul El-SayedAbdul El-Sayed, 42, won the Senate race in Michigan against Republican Mike Rogers, becoming the first Muslim Senator in U.S. history.His election was critical to the Democrats’ flipping control of the Senate and his campaign was hard-fought as he encountered a barrage of personal and Islamophobic attacks from Trump, who baselessly described El-Sayed as a member of the Muslim Brotherhood—an Islamist political movement—and repeatedly ridiculed his name.“Donald, look, I know you struggled with my name, so after [Vice President] J.D. [Vance] swears me in in January, you could just go on and call me ‘Senator,’” El-Sayed said in his victory speech.El-Sayed also faced an eleventh-hour setback when Haley Stevens, his Democratic primary opponent, endorsed Rogers the weekend before Election Day. The move was strongly criticized by members of the Democratic Party, with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jefferies putting his full support behind El-Sayed, who he described as a candidate that “will always put the American people first.” Despite those challenges, El-Sayed won Michigan, a state Trump had also carried in 2024, by seven points. He ran an unapologetically progressive and anti-establishment campaign, focusing in part on criticism of America's involvement in the Middle East and U.S. support for Israel.Masket argues that El-Sayed’s influence could make an impact ahead of the 2028 presidential race, particularly in the Midwest.“He could be a real kingmaker in the Midwest, and an influential person in the Democratic nomination, whose endorsement will matter a lot for a Democrat who wants to win Michigan,” he says. —Paras Griffin—Getty ImagesKeisha Lance BottomsKeisha Lance Bottoms, 56, made history after defeating Republican Rick Jackson in the race to succeed term-limited Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp. She will become the state's first Black governor and first woman governor, as well as the first Black woman to serve as governor of any U.S. state.Bottoms served as mayor of Atlanta from 2018 to 2022, including during the COVID-19 pandemic, before taking on several roles in former President Joe Biden's Administration, including as a senior adviser and head of the White House Office of Public Engagement.As the governor of the Peach State, Bottoms’ influence may prove vital for any candidate running for President, with Georgia being hard fought between Democrats and Republicans. Georgia backed Trump during his first run to the White House in 2016, but then pivoted to former President Joe Biden in 2020, only to return to Trump in 2024—turning into a bellwether state for the last three cycles.Bottoms’ victory returns the governor’s office to a Democrat for the first time in over two decades, and will provide the party with a powerful platform in a presidential battleground. It is also important to note, Belt says, that Georgia borders South Carolina, which was selected earlier this year to kick off the Democratic Party’s 2028 presidential nominating schedule, potentially giving Bottoms further leverage in the Sun Belt area of the country. “She will [likely] be courted by a number of different Democratic primary contenders and would-be's,” he predicts. —Heather Ainsworth—Getty ImagesJosh ShapiroJosh Shapiro, 53, comfortably won re-election as Pennsylvania governor against Republican Stacy Garrity by a margin of more than 20 points in the midterms. He had a tall task heading into Election Day, with the goal of flipping four congressional seats in the House and retaining a majority in the state House. This was more than achieved with the party flipping four GOP-held seats in the House of Representatives and increasing their majority in the state legislature to at least 111 seats. The party also managed to flip at least three seats of the state Senate, giving them a majority and allowing them to hold a trifecta in the commonwealth state.Shapiro’s victory further strengthens his standing as the Democrats make plans for 2028, and he is already considered to be a potential contender.“Shapiro wins [in Pennsylvania] statewide multiple times by very large margins, and that gives him an argument for winning the nomination,” says Masket. “It's an argument for his electability that not a lot of other candidates can claim.”Shapiro was previously considered a potential running mate for Harris in 2024, but she ultimately selected Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz. Still, the fact Shapiro was considered for the role underscored his importance in the Democratic Party and his leading influence in one of the country’s most competitive swing states. —Kamil Krzaczynski—Getty ImagesRob SandRob Sand, 44, defeated Republican Zach Lahn in Iowa's open gubernatorial race, succeeding Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds and becoming the first Democrat elected governor of the state since 2006.His campaign emphasized his rural roots and his career as state auditor, instead honing in on local issues rather than close identification with the national Democratic Party.Having a governor at the state level could be very useful for Democrats, Belt says. “If you have the electoral infrastructure of winning at the state level, your endorsement carries a tremendous advantage because you know how to win the state,” he adds. “You have the donors. You have the volunteer base, and somebody like that could be extremely influential.” Sand's influence heading into 2028 could also come from demonstrating how Democrats can compete beyond their strongest metropolitan areas, as well as from his governing record in a politically divided state.“Iowa is a state that Democrats had largely written off until pretty recently, as it swung hard toward Trump in the last decade,” Masket explains. “Democrats may be making a real play for trying to win Iowa [in 2028]. Sand will be key for that, and they'll be listening to his advice.” —Mikala Compton/The Austin American-Statesman—Getty ImagesGina HinojosaGina Hinojosa, 52, is another Democrat who made history Tuesday after defeating three-term Republican Gov. Greg Abbott in Texas.She will become the first Latina governor of Texas and its first Democratic governor since Ann Richards, who took office in 1991.Alongside Talarico, Hinojosa could play an important role in Democrats' efforts to make further gains in Texas by helping to mobilize voters. Masket says “a lot of Democratic candidates will be seeking her out for her advice on how to mobilize voters and how to get people to show up for women and for Latinas.” —Jim Vondruska—Getty ImagesAdam HamiltonHamilton is the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Kansas in 94 years, ending a long dry spell for the Democratic Party. Deep-red Kansas emerged as an unexpected Senate battleground ahead of the midterms, as Hamilton went head-to-head with Trump-backed Republican incumbent Roger Marshall.In a major upset to the GOP, Hamilton secured 50.9% of the vote to Marshall’s 46.1%, flipping the crucial Senate seat for the Democrats. Hamilton, the founding and senior pastor of one of the largest United Methodist churches in the U.S., has described himself as both a “liberal” and a “conservative.” He was a Republican for “most” of his life, and has identified with both parties during the past.“I became a Democrat during the Obama Administration, when he was running, and so for eight years I was a Democrat… I served in his Administration for a couple years, but then I went back to being a Republican,” he told ABC News last month, adding that he’s now proud to be a Democrat once more.“What matters to me more than the letter behind your name is who you are, what you stand for, your character, and I think there’s a lot of people like that in our state,” he said.Hamilton, 62, notably won endorsements from two of Kansas’ former GOP governors, Mike Hayden and Bill Graves ahead of the midterms.Hamilton’s more moderate approach and his eagerness to engage with voters across party aisles could make him a dependable figure for the Democratic Party as it attempts to build on its current momentum. “I think of [Hamilton] as the ‘preacher turn’ in Democratic politics,” says Belt. “For a long time, the moral high ground has been ceded to Republicans. It's not that Democrats don't have a morality or a sense of Christianity, or whatever religion it is, they have just preferred not to talk about it, and by not doing that, they have lost that connection with [some] voters.” Having experience speaking to large congregations also means that Hamilton has already proven himself to be an apt orator, which Belt says could incentivize the Democratic Party to give him a "very prominent speaking position" on the road for the 2028 campaign trail or perhaps even at the Democratic National Convention. —Jeff Wheeler/The Minnesota Star Tribune—Getty ImagesPete ButtigiegDespite not being on the ballot during this midterm cycle, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg was a fixture on the campaign trail ahead of the midterms, making valuable allies as he stumped for candidates across the country.Buttigieg, 44, has built a reputation as one of the party's most effective communicators, both on the campaign trail and through media appearances. Ahead of the 2024 election, he appeared on Jubilee’s Surrounded debate series, where he made the case for the Democratic Party's achievements to 25 undecided voters.Belt describes Buttigieg as an “incredibly effective messenger” who “connects with voters in a way that is just spectacular.” “Buttigieg is able to explain how policies have made people's lives worse and how policies make people's lives better,” Belt says, pointing to a recent video in which Buttigieg broke down the rising prices under Trump at a local Waffle House.“He just has that sort of personal touch, and he can speak at a high level without sounding condescending,” Belt says, which makes Buttigieg an “important voice for the Democrats.”In 2020, Buttigieg became the first openly gay candidate in history to win a presidential primary. He later suspended his presidential campaign to endorse Biden, but he has since kept the door open to another bid.“I don’t have any news to make about that right now,” he told WNDU in October, when asked if he plans to run again. He nevertheless remains a prominent figure in early Democratic nomination polling averages.
